t0.said: Sockets: how programs on different machines talk to each other.

w1.said: Threads inside one program share its memory. But a cyber-physical system is spread across machines: a controller on a Raspberry Pi, and an operator's laptop.

w2.said: They share no memory. The laptop cannot read the Pi's variables. All they can do is send each other bytes, over a network.

w3.said: A program's end of that link is a socket. It writes bytes into the socket and reads bytes out of it, much like a file.

a1.said: A socket is found by two things. The I P address picks the machine, like the street address of a building.

a2.said: The port picks one program on that machine, like the apartment number inside the building. A packet needs both.

a3.said: The loopback address, localhost, is this same machine, so a client and a server can be tested on one computer.

c1.said: Networked programs usually take one of two roles. The server starts first: it binds a port, and listens.

c2.said: The client knows the server's address and port, and connects. Three packets set up the connection.

c3.said: The server accepts, and gets a new socket just for this client. The laptop's question arrives right behind, and the Pi answers.

c4.said: Then both ends close. Every packet here was recorded from a real connection, and slowed down so you can follow it.

p1.said: A socket speaks one of two protocols. T C P is a reliable, ordered stream of bytes, over a connection.

p2.said: Those three packets are its handshake: sin, sin-ack, ack. After that, everything that arrives is acknowledged.

p3.said: U D P has no connection. Each datagram is sent on its own, with no handshake and no acknowledgements.

p4.said: The same question and answer over U D P is just two packets. Less work, and nothing is promised.

l1.said: The difference shows when the network misbehaves. Six messages cross a link that loses the third one, and delays the fifth.

l2.said: T C P notices the gap and sends the third again. The fourth is held back until the third arrives, so all six reach the program, in order.

l3.said: U D P just carries on. The third is gone for good, and the fifth arrives after the sixth. The program has to cope with that.

s1.said: Which to use depends on the data. Here the Pi sends the arm's pose to the laptop, a hundred times a second.

s2.said: The poses go over U D P and T C P at once, through a link that loses packets. The see-through arms show what the laptop receives, in slow motion.

s3.said: The U D P copy misses a sample now and then, but the next one is never far behind, so it stays live.

s4.said: The T C P copy gets every sample. But each loss holds up everything behind it, so the copy freezes, then jumps to catch up.

s5.said: So: T C P when every message must arrive, like a command to the robot. U D P when fresh but sometimes lost beats complete but late.

b1.said: One more thing about T C P catches almost everyone out. It carries a stream of bytes, not separate messages.

b2.said: Write ping, then pong, and a single read on the other side can return ping pong. The boundary between them is gone.

b3.said: It happened earlier, too: after the lost packet, one read returned the third and fourth messages together.

b4.said: So mark the boundaries yourself: end each message with a newline, or send its length first. U D P keeps them: one send, one receive.

k1.said: C plus plus has no sockets in its standard library. The operating system's own interface is long-winded, and different on Linux and Windows.

k2.said: A small library such as Simple Socket hides all that. This is a whole echo server: listen on a port, accept a client, read, and write it back.

k3.said: And the client: connect, write hello, and read the reply. Start the server, then the client, and it prints: server replied, hello.

o1.said: In short: an address and a port find the program. T C P delivers every byte, in order. U D P sends datagrams, and promises nothing.
